title: Evals, Testing, Errors & Cost
scopeHtml: Scope: the design document, eval grading methods, test levels and tracing, retriable vs terminal errors, tool errors, model routing, cost levers and multi-agent economics.

notes.title: Design document
notes.html:
What it is. A short file, usually a single markdown page, written before implementation that states what you're building and how you'll know it's right. It exists so you define correct instead of rationalizing whatever the model produces later. Every production layer in this module is built on it.

Four decisions, each concrete enough to check the built system against.

  1. Success criteria — what the feature must produce, in terms specific enough to grade. "Summarize the thread" can't be checked; "a two-sentence summary that lists every action item and its owner" can. These criteria are what your eval set is built from, so writing them first is what makes the eval possible.
  2. Failure handling — the failures the system must survive and what it does for each. List the errors production will throw, mark each retriable or terminal, and say what the user gets when a failure can't be recovered. Deciding this on paper stops the first real rate-limit response from being the moment you discover you have no error path.
  3. Cost and latency budget — the ceiling the system must stay under and the reliability floor it can't trade away. Write the per-request budget, the monthly cost ceiling, the latency target, and the minimum reliability the design must hold. Set hard budgets before architecture is determined so you can check the design against them before writing code.
  4. Trust boundary — which inputs are untrusted and what the system may do. Write down which content the agent reads that someone else can write, and the smallest set of actions and access the feature needs. This turns least privilege into a design decision enforceable with a hook rather than a setting you remember later.

How each decision feeds a layer. Success criteria → eval cases. Failures → retriable/terminal error handling. Budget → the numbers you instrument against and the floor you refuse to optimize below. Trust boundary → what is treated as data and what actions are gated.

With agentic coding tools. The document is also what you hand over before it writes anything: plan the work, capture it as an artifact, implement against it. A tool given clear criteria and constraints makes fewer assumptions and produces code you can check against the agreed document.

Real life. An architect's brief before pouring concrete.

Tech. An RFC / design doc with an SLO section.

notes.title: Evals and graders
notes.html:
What an eval is. The test set that defines what a feature must do before it ships. Collect a set of input cases, write down the expected behaviour for each, run the feature on every case, and grade the output against the expectation. "Done" stops being a feeling after a few manual tries and becomes a score on a fixed set of cases. Write it before the feature.

The pipeline is small. Load a dataset, run each case through the feature, grade each result, average the scores:

def run_test_case(tc):
    output = run_prompt(tc)
    return {"output": output, "test_case": tc, "score": grade(tc, output)}

def run_eval(dataset):
    results = [run_test_case(c) for c in dataset]
    print("Average score:", sum(r["score"] for r in results) / len(results))
    return results

What the score means. On its own it isn't good or bad: a first attempt scoring two or three out of ten is normal. What matters is whether it rises as you change the prompt, the tools or the model — one change at a time, so you know which caused the improvement. The eval is the instrument that makes change measurable instead of a matter of opinion. It is also the gate for a model decision (promote a tier change on a measured score).

Matching the grader to the output shape.

Output Grader What it catches Where it's unreliable
Single correct label or value Exact/string match A wrong answer when exactly one correct form exists; cheapest, zero ambiguity Fails every valid paraphrase or reordering; wrong for anything open-ended
Structured or code output Code-graded check (valid JSON, parses, in range, required field present) Format and syntax failures a string match misses Says nothing about whether the content is good
Open-ended quality LLM-as-judge (rubric, score with reasoning) Faithfulness, instruction-following, completeness, tone — nothing a code rule can express Noisy and costly; a confident-looking number that means nothing until calibrated

Examples. An array of three capitals in a different order scores 0 on exact match but passes a code check (parse + membership). A one-paragraph rationale: a code check only confirms it's non-empty; exact match is hopeless; only a judge can say whether it's faithful and complete.

A parse is a grader. json.loads success = pass, exception = fail catches a whole class of format failures cheaply (same for ast.parse on generated Python).

Cost and cadence. Exact and code graders run locally and cost nothing per case, so run thousands on every change. A judge is a second model call per case: a thousand-case eval is a thousand extra API calls each run. Run code graders on every commit and the judge on a slower scheduled quality pass.

Calibrating the judge. The judge is the only grader you must build and tune. Compare its scores to known-good and known-bad cases (and human labels), refine the rubric, and re-check when the judge model changes.

Coverage over perfection. Include edge cases, not just the demo path. In the "demo that passed" postmortem the feature passed every check it had and still extracted the wrong value on an edge case no check covered.

Real life. Exam marking: multiple choice is auto-marked (exact), a coding test runs against hidden tests (code check), an essay needs a calibrated examiner (judge).

Tech. Unit tests, schema validation and code review.

notes.title: Test levels and tracing
notes.html:
A test is only useful if you know which failure it identifies. Four levels divide the work, and most silent production breaks live at one particular level.

Level What it isolates What it can't catch
Unit one function (a parser, a tool wrapper) in isolation how pieces fit together
Functional one Claude call returns the expected shape for an input (right fields, type, parseable) the system around the call
Integration the handoff between two components (e.g. retrieval result → model call) full-flow effects
End-to-end the whole flow as a user would run it slow; hard to localize failures

The integration level is where most silent failures hide: each side can pass its own tests while the handoff between them is broken. In the "pieces passed, seam broke" case, prompt tests and parser unit tests were green, yet the end-to-end run failed because the model returned a field under a different name than the parser expected.

Tracing. Tests tell you a failure exists; a trace tells you where. A trace records each step: the prompt, tool calls, intermediate outputs and timing. It turns "the case failed" into "step four: the parser raised a KeyError on a field the model didn't return" — the difference between a five-minute fix and a day tracing by hand.

[trace run_id=8f21c] case: "Where is my refund?"
  step 1 retrieve(query)       ok   42ms  -> 3 chunks
  step 2 build_prompt(chunks)  ok    1ms  -> prompt 1,240 tok
  step 3 model.call(prompt)    ok  980ms  -> answer "..."
  step 4 parse(answer)         FAIL  2ms  -> KeyError: amount   (failure localized)

Routing between approaches. A cheap classification step can send single-fact lookups to fetch-once retrieval and multi-part questions to iterative search, so you pay for iteration only when needed; skip the router if all queries look alike.

Fix for seam failures. Constrain output with structured outputs/schema validation at the seam and add an integration test there.

Real life. Testing each car part on a bench passes; the car won't start because the wire between two parts is loose.

Tech. Contract tests between microservices.

notes.title: Errors and retries
notes.html:
Every failure starts with one question: would waiting and trying the exact same request again plausibly work? If yes it's retriable; if not it's terminal. A rate limit clears with time; a malformed request fails identically until the request is fixed.

Status classification.

RETRIABLE = {429, 529, 500, 502, 503, 504}   # rate limit, overload, transient server errors
TERMINAL  = {400, 401, 403, 404}             # bad request, auth, permission, missing

Decision table.

Error Class Backoff/handling Fallback
429 rate limit retriable exponential backoff with jitter, honor retry-after, cap attempts after the cap: clean error, or cached/simpler result
529 overloaded retriable backoff; reflects Anthropic-side load, not a rate-limit signal fail over to a fallback path or graceful error if persistent
500/502/503/504 retriable backoff as above
400 bad request terminal no retry; identical request fails again fix/reject input, surface the error
401/403/404 terminal no retry (403 is permissions; retry can't fix) fix credentials/permissions/target
Timeout usually retriable may have been too slow; repeated timeouts on expensive requests mean fix the request smaller work units
Tool failure depends retry only if the cause is transient return is_error: true to Claude
Refusal (HTTP 200, stop_reason: "refusal") terminal a status-code classifier will not catch it fail fast; review the input

Why classification matters. Retrying a terminal error wastes budget and hides the real problem behind a wall of identical failures; misclassifying a retriable error as terminal fails loudly and gets fixed. When unsure, treat as terminal and raise.

The SDK already retries. The client libraries automatically retry transient failures with progressive delays up to a configurable count. Before writing your own loop know what it covers: two loops around the same call multiply attempts against a rate limit instead of capping them. Either let the SDK handle transient cases and reserve your code for application-specific fallbacks, or turn SDK retries down and own the whole path.

retry-after. A 429/529 response includes it; honoring it is more precise than guessing with backoff alone. Use the header first and fall back to exponential backoff only when absent. Rate-limit header names and values are version-pinned; confirm.

Tool errors must come back explicitly. When a tool fails, return a tool_result with is_error: true and a useful message — never a silent empty result. The model treats an empty result as valid data and reasons onward on a false premise, producing a confident wrong answer; a visible failure is far easier to catch.

except Exception as e:
    return {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": tool_use.id,
            "is_error": True, "content": f"Tool failed: {e}"}

The call that never failed in development. In development the API never rate-limits; the first 429 in production took the whole request down because no error path existed. Decide failure handling in the design document.

Real life. A busy phone line (try again) versus a wrong number (no amount of redialing helps).

Tech. HTTP clients with jittered backoff and circuit breakers.

notes.title: Cost and routing
notes.html:
Model choice sets the baseline that cost optimization works within. Fable (most capable), Opus, Sonnet (balanced default), Haiku (speed and cost) trade cost, latency and capability; the same prompt runs on any, so model choice is a lever you set per workload.

The trade-off. Upgrading buys quality at higher per-token cost and usually higher latency; downgrading buys speed and lower cost at risk of a quality drop. A higher tier can occasionally finish faster and cheaper by reaching a conclusion in fewer tokens. The cost of a mistake belongs in the calculation: saving a few dollars a day isn't sound if errors carry large downstream cost.

Routing. A default model plus an override on a cheap signal read from the request (task type, input length, a difficulty classification): send the bulk to the balanced default and specific request types to a larger or smaller model. For uniform traffic at one quality bar, pin one model and skip the router (it adds a classification step and a second path to maintain).

Step up / step down. Step up when an eval shows the current tier failing the hardest cases and a wrong answer is costly; step down when an eval shows a cheaper model holding the bar on the bulk. The eval is the instrument in both directions.

Observability for cost. Instrument three metrics on every call — token usage (input and output), latency, error rate — via a thin wrapper that records the usage the API already returns. Then a cost spike becomes "which step, on which request type" instead of "why is the bill high". A flow that seems uniformly expensive usually has one step doing ~90% of the spend; that is where optimization effort belongs.

The levers.

  • Model selection (smaller, faster for simpler steps).
  • Prompt and context size (trim; retrieve instead of stuffing).
  • Number of tool calls.
  • Streamed vs batched (streaming helps perceived latency for a user; batching cuts cost for non-urgent work; they never compete for the same request).
  • Streaming with tool use: accumulate deltas by index until the stream closes, then reconstruct tool calls from completed blocks; don't act on a partial block.
  • Prompt caching (writes ~1.25x/2x, reads ~0.1x; stable prefixes; exact match).
  • The Batches API: lower cost, up to 24 h latency, right for scheduled/non-urgent work; batching and caching compound on jobs with shared context.

Reliability floor. The cheapest configuration is rarely the most reliable. Define the base first (retry budget, latency ceiling), then tune cost above it. Cutting below the floor replaces a visible expense with silent failures — a worse trade, because a slightly higher bill is easier to defend than a system that doesn't work.

Real life. A phone bill: you only cut it once you see which line uses the data.

Tech. Per-endpoint cost dashboards; autoscaling with a minimum replica count.

notes.title: Multi-agent economics
notes.html:
The pattern. In an orchestrator-worker setup a lead agent decomposes a task and delegates subtasks to several subagents working in parallel, each with its own context window; the lead then compiles results. In code: plan → parallel fan-out → synthesize.

plan = await lead.plan(task)
results = await gather(*[worker.run(s) for s in plan.subtasks])   # each spends its own tokens
return await lead.synthesize(results)

When it helps. Large tasks that split into independent parts, e.g. research across many separate sources, where subagents explore simultaneously rather than one after another.

What it costs. Anthropic's own research system reported a substantial improvement over a single-agent baseline on its internal eval (a multi-agent setup with a larger lead and smaller subagents versus a single larger agent) at roughly fifteen times the tokens of a normal chat interaction, because every subagent spends its own tokens against its own context. Their analysis found token usage explains most of the performance variance: the architecture works largely because it buys more parallel computation.

Rough estimate. A single agent answers a research question in ~10k tokens. A lead plus four subagents (five contexts plus a synthesis pass) → ~15x → on the order of 150k tokens. If the question was a single lookup dressed up as research, you paid the multiplier for nothing.

When it's a poor fit. Tightly coupled tasks such as coding, where each step depends on previous parts and can't be explored in parallel. A single agent with good context handles most work at a fraction of the cost. The multiplier compounds when something misbehaves (a runaway subagent or an oversized tool result can exceed 15x).

Failure handling multiplies too. Each subagent needs the same retriable-versus-terminal handling, backoff and fallback discipline, applied independently; a subagent that hits a rate limit with no backoff can stall the lead's synthesis forever. Orchestration doesn't replace failure-handling work, it multiplies it.

Right-sizing. Route by task: single-fact lookups to a single agent; reserve orchestrator-worker for broad splittable research; cap fan-out; per-request token budgets and alerts; consider smaller models for subagents.

Real life. Hiring five researchers: faster for a broad survey, but five salaries; wasteful for a single phone call.

Tech. MapReduce on a job that actually partitions versus a single-threaded query for one that doesn't.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Design doc. Success criteria (gradable), failure handling (retriable/terminal and user outcome), cost/latency budget with a reliability floor, trust boundary. They feed eval, error handling, instrumentation, and hooks/least privilege respectively.

Evals. Dataset + expectation + grader + average, written before the feature, one change at a time; early low scores are normal. Exact match (single correct form; brittle), code checks (structure; no quality signal), LLM judge (open-ended; noisy, costly, needs calibration). Code graders on every commit, judge on a schedule. Cover edge cases.

Test levels. Unit, functional, integration (handoffs; most silent failures), end-to-end (slow). Tracing localizes failures to a step. Constrain output at seams.

Errors. Retriable vs terminal: 429/529/5xx retry with backoff + jitter and retry-after, capped; 400/401/403/404 and refusals (HTTP 200, stop_reason: "refusal") fail fast. SDK already retries — don't stack loops. Tool failures return is_error: true, never empty results. Unsure → terminal.

Cost. Pick the model baseline by eval; default model + override routing; instrument tokens/latency/error rate on every call; find the dominant step; levers: model, context size, tool calls, streaming, caching, Batches (compound). Tune cost above the reliability floor.

Multi-agent. Orchestrator-worker ≈ 15x tokens; good for broad parallel research, bad for tightly coupled work (coding); failure handling multiplies; right-size and budget.

One-liners.

  • "No eval, no 'done'."
  • "Judges need calibration; code graders run on every commit."
  • "Retry transient, fail fast on terminal, and a 200 can still be a refusal."
  • "Find the 90% step before optimizing."

questions.promptHtml:
Why write the eval before building the feature?

  • A. Evals are required by the API
  • B. It forces you to define success first, so "done" is a score on a fixed set of cases rather than rationalizing whatever the model produced
  • C. It makes the model faster
  • D. It replaces unit tests

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. An eval is dataset + expected behavior + grader + average, and you change one variable at a time so you know what moved the score.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Without an eval, 'done' is a feeling after a few manual tries. The pipeline is small: load cases, run each through the feature, grade each, average. A first score of 2 or 3 out of 10 is normal; what matters is that it rises as you change one thing at a time (prompt, tools or model). It complements unit tests (D); it does not replace them.

questions.promptHtml:
Match the grader. (1) A classifier that must return one of five labels. (2) A feature that must return valid JSON with a required field. (3) A paragraph explaining a recommendation, judged for faithfulness.

  • A. (1) LLM judge, (2) exact match, (3) code check
  • B. (1) exact match, (2) code-graded check, (3) LLM-as-judge
  • C. (1) code check, (2) judge, (3) exact match
  • D. LLM judge for all three

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. One correct form → exact match; structural rule → code check; open-ended quality → judge.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Exact match is cheap but fails valid paraphrases and reorderings. Code checks catch syntax and format failures but say nothing about quality. A judge is the only scalable option for faithfulness but it is costly, noisy, and its numbers mean nothing until calibrated against known-good cases. Run code graders on every commit; schedule the judge for periodic quality passes.

questions.contextHtml: Your prompt tests pass. Your parser unit tests pass. In production, refund requests fail. A trace shows retrieval ok, prompt built ok, model call ok, parse(answer) raises KeyError: amount because the model returned the field under a different name.
questions.promptHtml:
Which test layer was missing, and what would have caught it?

  • A. More unit tests on the parser
  • B. An integration test of the model-output → parser handoff (and an end-to-end case), because each side passed alone
  • C. A larger model
  • D. Fewer tests

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adding more unit tests on the same pieces.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where in the trace does it fail? What did the model return?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Tolerate/normalize the field or enforce a schema.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Seam mismatch; prompt drift; model change.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay the failing case from the trace.
  5. Root cause: The seam between components was never tested together.
  6. Fix: Constrain output with structured outputs or a schema, add an integration test.
  7. Prevention: Keep traces for every eval run so failures localize to a step.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't rely solely on slow end-to-end tests.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Which level hides most silent failures? → Integration (handoffs).

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more unit tests.
  • Hire: integration test.
  • Strong hire: integration plus schema constraint plus tracing.

questions.promptHtml:
Classify these responses: 429, 529, 400, 401, and a 200 with stop_reason: "refusal".

  • A. All retriable
  • B. 429 and 529 retriable (backoff with jitter, honor retry-after); 400 and 401 terminal; the refusal is terminal and a status-code classifier will not catch it
  • C. 400 retriable, 529 terminal
  • D. Only 429 is retriable

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Ask: would waiting and retrying the identical request plausibly work?

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Retriable: 429, 529, 500, 502, 503, 504. Terminal: 400, 401, 403, 404. A 529 is Anthropic-side load, not a rate-limit signal, and needs a fallback if persistent. When unsure, treat as terminal so the failure is loud. The SDK already retries transient failures, so do not nest your own loop on top (attempts multiply); pick one layer.

questions.promptHtml:
A tool throws an exception. What should the loop return to Claude?

  • A. An empty tool_result
  • B. Nothing; skip the block
  • C. A tool_result with the matching tool_use_id, is_error: true and a clear message, so Claude can react
  • D. A refusal

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: C. An empty result is treated as valid data and produces a confident, wrong answer.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The model treats an empty result as valid data and keeps reasoning on a false premise, producing a confident but wrong answer. Returning is_error: true with a message lets Claude try another approach, ask for clarification or stop. Skipping the block (B) breaks the tool_use/tool_result pairing rule.

questions.promptHtml:
Spend is high and nobody knows why. What is the first step?

  • A. Switch to the cheapest model
  • B. Instrument every call (input tokens, output tokens, latency, error rate) so you can find the one step that accounts for most spend
  • C. Remove all tools
  • D. Disable caching

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Optimizing the wrong step is wasted effort; usually one step is ~90% of the bill.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Then pull the right lever: model routing (default model with an override on a cheap signal such as task type), prompt/context size, number of tool calls, caching for stable prefixes, Batches for non-urgent work (batch discount and caching compound). Define the reliability floor (retry budget, latency ceiling) first and tune cost above it, never below.

questions.contextHtml: A team replaced a single research agent (about 10k tokens per question) with a lead agent plus four parallel subagents. Quality is slightly better; the bill is roughly 15x. Many questions are single-fact lookups.
questions.promptHtml:
What is the best response?

  • A. Keep it; multi-agent is always better
  • B. Route by task: single-fact lookups to one agent, reserve orchestrator-worker for broad, splittable research, and give each subagent its own retry/backoff
  • C. Add more subagents
  • D. Use orchestrator-worker for coding tasks too

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Treating the 15x as acceptable regardless of task shape.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What share of traffic is simple? What is quality vs cost per class?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap fan-out.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Over-delegation; oversized tool results per subagent; runaway worker.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per-step token logs.
  5. Root cause: Paying for four extra contexts the task did not need.
  6. Fix: B, plus a cheap classifier router.
  7. Prevention: Per-request token budgets and alerts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't use it for tightly coupled work (coding), where steps depend on each other.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • A worker hits a rate limit with no backoff? → It can stall the lead's synthesis; orchestration multiplies failure handling.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts the bill.
  • Hire: routes.
  • Strong hire: routes, bounds fan-out, adds per-worker retries and budgets.

questions.promptHtml:
Which four decisions belong in the pre-code design document?

  • A. Logo, color, name, price
  • B. Success criteria, failure handling (retriable/terminal), cost and latency budget with a reliability floor, and the trust boundary
  • C. Model name, temperature, top_p, top_k
  • D. Team roster and timeline

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Each feeds a later layer: criteria → eval, failures → error handling, budget → instrumentation, trust boundary → hooks and least privilege.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Success criteria become the eval cases; failure handling becomes the retriable/terminal paths; the cost and latency budget (with a reliability floor) becomes what you instrument against; the trust boundary becomes what you treat as data and gate with hooks. Writing them once before building keeps every layer solving the same problem.

questions.promptHtml:
Which success criterion can an eval actually grade?

  • A. "Summarize the thread well"
  • B. "A two-sentence summary that lists every action item and its owner"
  • C. "Be helpful"
  • D. "Sound professional"

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. It is specific enough to check.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Vague goals cannot be graded. The criteria in the design document are what the eval set is built from, so writing them first is what makes the eval possible.

questions.promptHtml:
Why does an exact-match grader score zero on a correct JSON array whose items are in a different order?

  • A. The array is wrong
  • B. Exact match compares characters, so valid reorderings and paraphrases fail; a code check on membership would pass it
  • C. JSON is not comparable
  • D. The model failed

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Exact match is cheapest but most brittle.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Use it only when one correct form exists.

questions.promptHtml:
What does a code-graded check NOT tell you?

  • A. Whether the output is valid JSON
  • B. Whether the content is good, only whether it is well-formed
  • C. Whether a field exists
  • D. Whether a number is in range

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Format and syntax yes, quality no.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A parse attempt is often enough to catch a whole class of format failures cheaply.

questions.promptHtml:
A team trusts an LLM judge's average of 8.4. What must they do first?

  • A. Nothing
  • B. Calibrate it against known-good and known-bad cases, since an uncalibrated score is a confident-looking number that means nothing
  • C. Raise the temperature
  • D. Use a smaller judge

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The judge is the only grader you must build and tune.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: It is also costly and noisy, so run it on a schedule while code graders run on every commit.

questions.promptHtml:
After changing both the prompt and the model, the score rose. What is the problem?

  • A. None
  • B. You cannot tell which change caused it; change one thing at a time
  • C. Scores can't rise
  • D. The model is too strong

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The eval makes change measurable only if changes are isolated.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The same eval gates model promotion: a tier change is accepted on a measured score against your cases.

questions.promptHtml:
What does a trace give you that a failed eval score does not?

  • A. A higher score
  • B. The step where the failure originated (prompt, tool call, intermediate output, timing)
  • C. A cheaper model
  • D. Nothing

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. It turns "the case failed" into "step four: the parser raised a KeyError".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Without a trace, a failed eval tells you something is wrong but not where.

questions.promptHtml:
Your code retries three times on 429, and the SDK already retries twice. Effect?

  • A. Total of three attempts
  • B. Attempts multiply against the rate limit; pick one layer to own retries
  • C. No effect
  • D. Errors disappear

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Two loops around the same call multiply rather than cap attempts.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Honor retry-after when present and fall back to exponential backoff with jitter.

questions.promptHtml:
A response comes back HTTP 200 with stop_reason: "refusal". How should code treat it?

  • A. Retry it as a transient failure
  • B. Fail fast: your status-code classifier will not catch it, so check stop_reason explicitly
  • C. Ignore it
  • D. Parse it as JSON

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Retrying the identical request will not change a refusal.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Surface it for review of the input.

questions.promptHtml:
Mixed traffic: most requests are easy, some are hard. What pattern saves money?

  • A. Always use the top tier
  • B. A default balanced model with an override to a larger or smaller model on a cheap task signal
  • C. Random assignment
  • D. Always Haiku

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. You pay for the capable model only where needed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: If all requests have the same shape, skip the router and pin one model.

questions.promptHtml:
The team cuts the retry budget and latency ceiling to save money. What is wrong?

  • A. Nothing
  • B. Cost should be tuned above a defined reliability floor; cutting below it swaps a visible bill for silent failures
  • C. Retries are free
  • D. Latency doesn't matter

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. A slightly higher bill is easier to defend than a system that does not work.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The reasoning and a real-world analogy are in the master notes section "cost and routing". Use the Source button to jump there.
